```{r setup}
library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(knitr); library(stringr)
library(flextable)

## Tables are rendered with flextable rather than kable: a pipe table leaves
## Word to guess the column widths, which squeezes the numeric columns of wide
## tables and breaks figures such as "15,094" across two lines. The caption is
## the table's first header row, because Quarto drops a flextable caption in
## Word output.
tbl <- function(df, caption, align = NULL) {
  x <- flextable(df) |>
    theme_booktabs() |>
    font(fontname = "Times New Roman", part = "all") |>
    fontsize(size = 10, part = "all") |>
    bold(part = "header") |>
    padding(padding.top = 1, padding.bottom = 1, part = "all") |>
    set_table_properties(layout = "autofit", width = 1,
                         opts_word = list(split = FALSE, keep_with_next = TRUE))
  if (!is.null(align)) x <- align(x, j = seq_along(align), align = align, part = "all")
  add_header_lines(x, caption) |>
    bold(i = 1, part = "header") |>
    align(i = 1, part = "header", align = "left") |>
    fontsize(i = 1, size = 10, part = "header") |>
    hline(i = 1, part = "header", border = officer::fp_border(color = "black", width = 1))
}

## Figures: PLOS wants the caption in the text and the figure uploaded as a
## separate file, which is hard to read in draft. A plain render therefore puts
## each figure under its caption; the submission build sets U5M_PLOS=1, which
## leaves the captions standing alone.
## "Wealth quintile: Poorest" reads badly when the variable name repeats down a
## whole block. Split it into a Characteristic column printed once per block and
## a Category column, the same shape as Table 1.
split_term <- function(df, col = "Term") {
  parts <- strsplit(as.character(df[[col]]), ": ", fixed = TRUE)
  ch <- vapply(parts, function(p) if (length(p) > 1) p[1] else "", character(1))
  ca <- vapply(parts, function(p) if (length(p) > 1) paste(p[-1], collapse = ": ") else p[1],
               character(1))
  cbind(data.frame(Characteristic = ifelse(duplicated(ch) & nzchar(ch), "", ch),
                   Category = ca, check.names = FALSE),
        df[setdiff(names(df), col)])
}

## a Monte Carlo p-value from R replicates cannot fall below 1/(R + 1)
pmc <- function(p, R = 999) {
  if (as.numeric(p) <= 1 / (R + 1) + 1e-9) paste0("\u2264 ", f3(1 / (R + 1)))
  else paste0("= ", f3(p))
}

}

  sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f (", lab, " %.", d, "f\u2013%.", d, "f)"), est, lo, hi)
}

  s <- sprintf(paste0("%+.", d, "f"), x)                 # that rounds to zero is
  s[as.numeric(s) == 0] <- formatC(0, format = "f", digits = d)   # printed unsigned
  sub("^-", "\u2212", s)
}
nw  <- function(n) {                                                      # numbers below 11 as words

  if (!is.na(n) && n >= 0 && n <= 10)
    c("zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")[n + 1]
  else format(n, big.mark = ",")
}

credible <- function(pattern, data = ifix) {
  r <- or_row(pattern, data); isTRUE(r$or_lo > 1 || r$or_hi < 1)
}
```

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

National averages hide where children in Nepal still die. District estimates
from a single survey are too imprecise to guide planning. This study estimated
under-five mortality for Nepal's 77 districts over two decades and tested
whether the gap between districts narrowed. Birth histories from the 2011, 2016
and 2022 Nepal Demographic and Health Surveys were pooled
(`r n_fmt(key[["n_births"]])` live births) and analysed as discrete-time
survival data. Spatial clustering was assessed with empirical-Bayes Moran's I
and a space-time scan statistic. A Bayesian spatio-temporal model estimated
district relative risks for four birth cohorts. A Bayesian individual-level
model estimated adjusted odds ratios (ORs). Four machine-learning models were
compared on held-out children and provinces. Under-five mortality fell from
`r f1(nat$u5mr[1])` to `r f1(tail(nat$u5mr, 1))` per 1,000 live births between
the `r P1d` and `r PLd` cohorts. Mortality was spatially clustered (Moran's
I = `r f2(mp$moran_I)`). One space-time cluster of `r sc1$n_districts`
districts in `r sc_provinces` had `r f2(sc1$rr)` times the expected risk.
Between-district dispersion did not change (posterior change
`r sgn(cL$change_median)`, 95% credible interval `r sgn(cL$change_lo)` to
`r sgn(cL$change_hi)`). Multiple birth, short birth intervals and no maternal
education were the strongest predictors. A modest district effect remained
after adjustment (median `r or_txt(mor_d$median_odds_ratio, mor_d$lo, mor_d$hi)`).
Machine learning did not outperform penalised regression. Nepal's national
decline was not accompanied by geographical convergence. Persistently high-risk
districts need more intensive, not different, intervention.

\newpage

# Introduction

Global under-five mortality has more than halved since 2000. Yet an estimated
4.8 million children died before their fifth birthday in 2023
[@igme2025]. Many countries remain off track for the Sustainable Development
Goal (SDG) target of no more than 25 deaths per 1,000 live births by 2030
[@sdg3]. Nepal has made large gains. Under-five mortality fell from more than
100 per 1,000 live births in the mid-1990s [@sreeramareddy2013] to 33 per 1,000
in the five years before the 2022 Nepal Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS) [@ndhs2022]. Community-based child health programmes, delivered by Female
Community Health Volunteers, contributed to this progress [@khatri2017].
Nepal's national SDG roadmap sets a stricter target than the global one: 20
deaths per 1,000 live births by 2030, with a milestone of 24 by 2025
[@npc2017].

National averages hide large differences within the country. Nepal's terrain
ranges from lowland plains to high Himalayan districts. Access to health
services varies greatly across this terrain. Earlier NDHS analyses found
persistent regional and socioeconomic inequalities in under-five mortality
[@sreeramareddy2013; @ghimire2019]. Mortality was highest among Terai/Madhesi
Dalit children and in Madhesh, Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces
[@ghimire2019fa]. Since the 2015 constitution, health services have been run by
seven provinces and 753 local governments [@thapa2019; @adhikari2022]. These
governments need sub-national evidence. However, a single NDHS round samples
only about 100 births per district. District rates from one survey are
therefore too imprecise to rank districts or to allocate resources.

Bayesian hierarchical models address this problem. They borrow strength from
neighbouring areas and adjacent time periods [@besag1991; @riebler2016;
@knorrheld2000]. They can be fitted quickly with integrated nested Laplace
approximation (INLA) [@rue2009;@blangiardo2013]. They are widely used to
estimate sub-national child mortality [@mercer2015; @golding2017;
@burstein2019; @zondi2023; @gascoigne2025; @fenta2025]. In Nepal, Bayesian
space-time models have been applied to childhood diarrhoea [@li2020], and
district trends in stunting have been mapped [@nepali2022]. No study was found
that estimated district-level under-five mortality across successive NDHS
rounds.

Evidence on the predictors of under-five mortality in Nepal comes mainly from
regression analyses [@ghimire2019; @bhusal2022; @bhusal2025]. Machine-learning
methods can capture interactions and non-linear effects. They are increasingly
applied to Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) data and interpreted with
Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) [@lundberg2017; @lundberg2020;
@naznin2025; @asnake2026; @bitew2026]. Some of these studies report
near-perfect accuracy, above 0.99 in one recent analysis [@naznin2025]. But
reported accuracy depends heavily on how models are evaluated. Treating death
before age five as a yes/no outcome ignores children who have not yet reached
age five. Splitting children from the same survey cluster between training and
test data overstates performance [@roberts2017]. A systematic review of
clinical prediction models found no advantage of machine learning over
logistic regression in well-conducted studies [@christodoulou2019].

This study pooled three NDHS rounds with four aims: (i) to estimate
district-level under-five mortality for four birth cohorts from 2002 to 2022;
(ii) to test whether the gap between districts narrowed; (iii) to identify
predictors of death and measure the district variation that remains after
adjustment; and (iv) to compare machine-learning and regression models, and to
test whether the importance of predictors differs between provinces.

# Materials and methods

## Data

The study used three nationally representative surveys: the 2011, 2016 and
2022 NDHS [@ndhs2011; @ndhs2016; @ndhs2022]. Each survey used stratified
multistage cluster sampling. Women aged 15--49 years reported a complete birth
history. For every live birth, it records the date of birth and survival
status, and, for children who died, the age at death. The birth recode files
contained `r n_fmt(gsub("[^0-9]", "", tb("tableS_sample_flow")[[2]][1]))` birth
records. They were linked to the cluster GPS files. Reporting follows the
STROBE statement [@strobe2007]. The prediction-model component follows
TRIPOD+AI [@tripodai2024]. The STROBE checklist is given in S1 Checklist and the TRIPOD+AI checklist in
S2 Checklist.

All dates in the Nepal recodes use the Bikram Sambat calendar. Ages, exposure
times and birth intervals are differences between two dates, so they are
unaffected. Calendar years were converted to the Gregorian calendar before
births were assigned to cohorts (Section S1 in S1 File).

## Linking clusters to districts

The DHS displaces cluster coordinates for confidentiality: by up to 2 km in
urban areas, 5 km in rural areas and 10 km for 1% of rural clusters
[@burgert2013]. Each cluster was placed in one of Nepal's 77 districts by
overlaying its coordinates on the post-2015 district boundaries. A
nearest-district rule was prepared for points outside every district, but no
point needed it. Province was assigned from the district. Cluster altitude came
from the DHS elevation data. Fig S1 in S1 File shows the study area.

## Study population and outcome

The study included live births in the 120 months before interview, born from
2002 to 2022. The analytic sample had `r n_fmt(key[["n_births"]])` children in
`r n_fmt(key[["n_clusters"]])` clusters. Of these, `r n_fmt(key[["n_deaths"]])`
died before age five (Table S1 and Fig S2 in S1 File). A ten-year window was
used because district estimates need more births than the usual five-year
window. Births occurred in `r key[["n_districts"]]` districts. Manang and Rukum
East were not sampled in any round, so their estimates come entirely from the
spatial model.

Each child was followed from birth until death, the fifth birthday or the
interview, whichever came first. The child contributed one record for each of
the eight DHS age segments entered: 0, 1--2, 3--5, 6--11, 12--23, 24--35, 36--47
and 48--59 months [@singer1993]. The outcome was death within the segment.
Follow-up stopped at the age reached at interview. Children born shortly
before a survey therefore contributed only the ages they had lived through
(Fig S3 in S1 File). This gave `r n_fmt(key[["n_person_period"]])` records
with `r n_fmt(key[["n_deaths"]])` deaths. Births were grouped into four
five-year birth cohorts (`r and_list(dash(PERIODS))`). Each survey covers the
previous ten years. The two middle cohorts therefore draw on two surveys, and
the outer cohorts on one.

## Mortality rates

Neonatal, infant and under-five mortality were calculated with the DHS
life-table method [@dhsguide]. For each age segment $i$, the probability of
dying $q_i$ is the weighted number of deaths divided by the weighted number of
children entering the segment, less half of those censored within it. The
probability of dying before age five is $1 - \prod_i (1 - q_i)$. Because
children were grouped by birth cohort, these are cohort rates, not the period
rates published in NDHS reports. Survey weights were applied to all mortality rates and to Table 1. The
weights were normalised within each survey, so each round contributes in
proportion to its sample size. Confidence intervals (CIs) came from 300
bootstrap samples of survey clusters within each survey round.

## Covariates

Covariates followed the Mosley--Chen framework [@mosleychen1984]:

- **Child:** sex, multiple birth, birth order and preceding birth interval,
  with first births identified separately.
- **Mother:** age at the birth, education, employment, exposure to mass media
  and caste/ethnicity.
- **Household:** wealth, urban or rural residence, sex of household head,
  drinking-water source, sanitation, electricity and cooking fuel.
- **Place and time:** province, cluster altitude, birth cohort and survey
  round.

Caste/ethnicity was coded in the same way in all three surveys. It was grouped
into the seven categories used in DHS analyses for Nepal [@ghimire2019fa]:
Brahmin/Chhetri, Terai/Madhesi other castes, Dalit, Newar, Janajati, Muslim and
other.

Two common variables were excluded because a child's death changes them. The
number of children ever born rises when a mother replaces a child who died
[@palloni1999]. Household size falls after a death, because a dead child is no
longer a household member. Both are recorded after any death, so both partly
encode the outcome. They were used only in a sensitivity analysis.

```{r nrshare}
#| include: false
t1x <- tb("table1_characteristics")
numify <- function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(gsub("[, ]", "", x)))
wrow <- function(cat) t1x[t1x$Characteristic == "Drinking-water source" & t1x$Category == cat, ]
## Table 1 columns (07_tables.R): Births, Wt %, Deaths, U5MR
nr_n   <- numify(wrow("Not recorded")[["Births"]])
nr_pct <- numify(wrow("Not recorded")[["Wt %"]])
nr_u5  <- numify(wrow("Not recorded")[["U5MR"]])
imp_u5 <- numify(wrow("Improved")[["U5MR"]])
uni_u5 <- numify(wrow("Unimproved")[["U5MR"]])
eth_u5 <- function(cat)
  numify(t1x[t1x$Characteristic == "Caste/ethnicity" & t1x$Category == cat, "U5MR"])
## a renamed column returns NULL, which prints as empty text rather than an
## error, so fail loudly instead
stopifnot("Table 1 values for the 'not recorded' paragraph are missing; check column names" =
            all(lengths(list(nr_n, nr_pct, nr_u5, imp_u5, uni_u5)) == 1),
          "Table 1 caste/ethnicity values are missing; check column names" =
            length(eth_u5("Dalit")) == 1 && length(eth_u5("Brahmin/Chhetri")) == 1)
```

Water, sanitation, cooking fuel and electricity were not recorded for women who
were visitors in the sampled household (`r n_fmt(nr_n)` children,
`r f1(nr_pct)`%). These children came from all wealth groups. Their under-five
mortality (`r f1(nr_u5)` per 1,000) lay between that of children with improved
(`r f1(imp_u5)`) and unimproved (`r f1(uni_u5)`) water sources (Table 1). They
were therefore kept as a separate "not recorded" group. The same children were
unrecorded for all four variables. In the regression models, the four
identical "not recorded" indicators were replaced by one indicator.

## Spatial clustering

A district-cohort cell contained about 100 sampled births, so crude rates are
unstable. Rates were therefore also smoothed with the empirical-Bayes method
[@marshall1991]. Global spatial autocorrelation was measured on smoothed rates with
Moran's I. Districts sharing a border were treated as neighbours, and each
test used 9,999 random permutations. Local clusters were identified with the
Getis--Ord Gi\* statistic [@getisord1992], at p < 0.05 and after
Benjamini--Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction for the 77 tests
[@benjamini1995]. Geary's C, the Assunção--Reis empirical-Bayes index
[@assuncao1999] and local Moran's I [@anselin1995] were also computed. They
gave the same picture and are reported in S1 File.

Space-time clusters were detected with a discrete Poisson Kulldorff scan
statistic [@kulldorff1997; @kulldorff1998]. Each scanning window combined a
circle of neighbouring districts with one or two consecutive birth cohorts. A
window could cover at most half of the expected deaths and half of the study
period. Expected deaths used the national mortality schedule for the same age
segment and birth cohort. A cluster therefore shows mortality that is high
compared with the rest of Nepal at the same time, not the national decline.
Significance was tested with 999 Monte Carlo replications, so the smallest
possible p-value is 0.001.

## Bayesian spatio-temporal model

Deaths $y_{it}$ in district $i$ and cohort $t$ were modelled as
$y_{it} \sim \text{Poisson}(E_{it}\,\theta_{it})$. Here $E_{it}$ is the
expected number of deaths and $\theta_{it}$ is the relative risk (RR) compared
with the national level in the same cohort. The model for $\log \theta_{it}$
had three parts:

- an intercept;
- a BYM2 district effect, which combines a spatially structured and an
  unstructured component, with a mixing parameter $\phi$ [@besag1991;
  @riebler2016];
- a first-order random walk over cohorts.

Four further models added one of the Knorr-Held space-time interactions
[@knorrheld2000]. Penalised-complexity priors were used [@simpson2017], with
$\Pr(\sigma > 1) = 0.01$ for each standard deviation and $\Pr(\phi < 0.5) =
0.5$. Models were fitted with INLA [@rue2009]. They were compared with the
deviance information criterion (DIC), the widely applicable information
criterion (WAIC) and the cross-validated log score. For every district and
cohort, the posterior probability that RR exceeded 1.2 was calculated.
Probabilities above 0.8 were taken as strong evidence of an excess of at least
20%.

To test whether districts converged, the standard deviation of log RR across
districts was calculated in each cohort. This was repeated in each of 1,000
joint posterior samples. The result is a credible interval for the dispersion
and for its change since `r P1d`. This approach avoids a false appearance of
convergence. Posterior means are pulled towards the national level most
strongly in cohorts with fewer births, and comparing them would make districts
look more alike.

## Individual-level model

Predictors were studied with a Bayesian discrete-time survival model. It was
fitted to the child-age-segment records with a logit link. The model included
the age segment, all covariates, a BYM2 district effect and a random effect for
survey cluster. Fixed effects had normal priors with mean 0 and variance 10.
Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) are reported with 95% credible intervals (CrIs). The
remaining variation between districts was summarised by the median OR
[@merlo2006]. It was calculated over the posterior distribution of the district
precision.

Three sensitivity analyses were run:

1. a survey-weighted logistic regression with design-based standard errors for
   strata and clusters [@lumley2004];
2. the main model restricted to births in the five years before interview,
   which are less affected by recall error;
3. the main model with the number of children ever born and household size
   added.

## Machine learning

Four models were compared: elastic-net logistic regression [@friedman2010],
random forest [@breiman2001; @wright2017], gradient boosting [@chen2016] and a
stacked ensemble of the three [@vanderlaan2007]. The models predicted death
within each age segment from the covariates above. Each variable was entered
once, as a continuous variable where available. Survey weights were not used.

Children were randomly assigned to a training set (70%) and a test set (30%).
The split was stratified by outcome and survey round. Model settings were chosen by random search: 12 configurations for gradient boosting and 6 for random forest. The training set
was divided into ten groups of children. Each configuration was trained on nine
groups and scored on the tenth, and this was repeated for five of the ten
groups. The setting with the highest area under the precision-recall curve
(AUPRC) was chosen. The stacked ensemble was fitted to ten-fold out-of-fold
predictions (Tables S9 and S10 in S1 File). The test set was used only once,
for the final evaluation.

Only `r f1(100 * best_row$prevalence)`% of records ended in death. Accuracy was
therefore measured with both the AUPRC and the area under the receiver
operating characteristic curve (AUROC) [@saito2015]. Calibration was measured
with the Brier score, the calibration intercept and slope, and decile plots
[@vancalster2019]. Class weighting during training inflates predicted risks, so
the tree models were recalibrated by Platt scaling [@platt1999]. The scaling was
fitted to training-set predictions and does not change the AUROC or AUPRC. CIs
came from bootstrap samples of children.

Segment risks $h_s$ were also combined into each child's risk of dying before
age five, $1 - \prod_s (1 - h_s)$. This was evaluated among children whose
outcome was known: those who died, and those whose fifth birthday was observed.
Transfer between regions was tested by leave-one-province-out validation: each
model was trained on six provinces and tested on the seventh [@roberts2017].
The gradient-boosting model, refitted to the full sample, was interpreted with
TreeSHAP values [@lundberg2020]. SHAP values were summed within each
categorical variable and were also summarised by province.

## Software and ethics

Analyses were performed in R `r paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".")`
[@rcore] with the packages sf [@pebesma2018], spdep [@bivand2018], INLA,
survey [@lumley2004], glmnet, ranger, xgboost and shapviz. Package versions are
given in Table S20 in S1 File. A fixed random seed was used for all random
steps.

This is a secondary analysis of anonymised data obtained from the DHS Program
under a data-use agreement. The NDHS protocols were approved by the Nepal Health
Research Council and the ICF Institutional Review Board. Informed consent was
obtained from all respondents. No further ethical approval was required.

## Sample and national trends

The analytic sample comprised `r n_fmt(key[["n_births"]])` live births in
`r n_fmt(key[["n_clusters"]])` clusters. They contributed
`r n_fmt(key[["n_person_period"]])` child-age-segment records and
`r n_fmt(key[["n_deaths"]])` under-five deaths (Table 1).

Under-five mortality fell from `r f1(nat$u5mr[1])` per 1,000 live births in the
`r P1d` cohort to `r f1(tail(nat$u5mr, 1))` in the `r PLd` cohort. This is a
decline of `r f1(key[["pct_decline"]])`% (Table 2; Fig 1A). Neonatal mortality
fell more slowly, from `r f1(nat$nnmr[1])` to `r f1(tail(nat$nnmr, 1))` per
1,000. As a result, the share of under-five deaths in the first month rose
from `r f1(100 * nat$nnmr[1] / nat$u5mr[1])`% to
`r f1(100 * tail(nat$nnmr, 1) / tail(nat$u5mr, 1))`%. Trends by province are
shown in Fig S6 in S1 File.

## Spatial clustering

Pooled over 2002--2022, district under-five mortality was spatially clustered.
On empirical-Bayes rates, Moran's I was `r f3(mp$moran_I)` (p
`r pfmt(mp$moran_p)`; Table S3 in S1 File). Within single cohorts, the evidence
was weaker.
Moran's I was significant in `r nw(sum(mper_raw$moran_p < 0.05))` of four
cohorts on crude rates and in `r nw(sum(mper_eb$moran_p < 0.05))` on smoothed
rates (Table S3 in S1 File). Single-cohort district rates carry little
information (Fig S4 in S1 File). Getis--Ord Gi\* found `r nw(n_hot)`
hot-spot and `r nw(n_cold)` cold-spot districts at p < 0.05. After FDR
correction, `r nw(n_hotf)` hot spots and `r if (n_coldf == 0) "no" else nw(n_coldf)` cold spots remained
(Fig 2A; Table S4 and Fig S5 in S1 File).


The scan statistic found one significant space-time cluster (Table 3; Fig 2B).
It comprised `r sc1$n_districts` neighbouring districts in `r sc_provinces`
(`r sc_districts`) in the `r sc_cohorts` cohorts. The cluster had
`r sc1$observed` observed deaths against `r f1(sc1$expected)` expected (RR
`r f2(sc1$rr)`, p `r pmc(sc1$p_value)`). No other cluster was significant.

## Bayesian spatio-temporal model

The `r best_inla` model had the lowest DIC (Table 4). Its advantage over the
model without a space-time interaction was only `r f1(dic_gap)` units, which is
too small to matter. The Type IV model fitted poorly, with `r typeiv_fail`
cross-validation failures. The spatial pattern was therefore nearly fixed over
time: the same districts stayed above or below the national level while
mortality fell everywhere. The BYM2 mixing parameter was
`r ci_txt(phi$mean, phi$lower, phi$upper)`. Its wide interval means the data
cannot say precisely how much of the district variation is spatially
structured (Table S5 in S1 File).

```{r tbl5}
tbl(tb("table7_model_comparison"),
    caption = "Table 4. Comparison of Bayesian spatio-temporal models for district-cohort under-five deaths. Lower DIC, WAIC and mean log score indicate better fit.")
```

Posterior mortality was highest in the districts of Karnali and Sudurpashchim.
It was lowest in the Kathmandu Valley and nearby districts of Bagmati and
Gandaki (Fig 3). In the `r PLd` cohort, the highest relative risks were in
`r top_burden`. In total, `r nw(n_exceed)` districts had a posterior
probability above 0.8 of exceeding the national level by more than 20%
(Fig 4A and B; Tables S6 and S7 in S1 File).

## Predictors of under-five mortality

In the adjusted Bayesian model (Table 6), higher odds of death were associated
with `r results_or`. `r pred_extra`

```{r tbl7}

    align = c("left", "left", "right", "right"),
```

After adjustment, the median OR between districts was
`r ci_txt(mor_d$median_odds_ratio, mor_d$lo, mor_d$hi)`. Between clusters it was
`r ci_txt(mor_c$median_odds_ratio, mor_c$lo, mor_c$hi)`. Both are given in
Table S16 in S1 File. The largest residual district effects were in Karnali and Sudurpashchim
(Fig 4C). The district effect was
modest`r if (mor_d$median_odds_ratio < mor_c$median_odds_ratio) " and smaller than the cluster effect" else ""`.
But its credible interval excluded 1. Measured child, maternal and household
characteristics therefore did not fully explain the differences between
districts.

The survey-weighted model and the five-year model gave similar estimates
(Tables S17 and S18 in S1 File).
`r if (n_same_dir == nrow(same_dir)) paste0("All ", nw(nrow(same_dir))) else paste(nw(n_same_dir), "of the", nw(nrow(same_dir)))`
key associations had the same direction in the five-year model. Adding
children ever born and household size gave ORs per standard deviation of
`r ci_txt(par_add$or, par_add$or_lo, par_add$or_hi)` and
`r ci_txt(hh_add$or, hh_add$or_lo, hh_add$or_hi)`. These directions are
expected if the two variables partly reflect the death itself. Adding them
also weakened the associations with no maternal education (OR
`r f2(or_row("^meduNone", sens[sens$analysis == ADD, ])$or)`) and the poorest
wealth quintile (OR `r f2(or_row("^wealthPoorest", sens[sens$analysis == ADD, ])$or)`).
Outcome-dependent variables can therefore hide socioeconomic gradients.

# Discussion

This study pooled three NDHS rounds to estimate district-level under-five
mortality in Nepal across four birth cohorts. Under-five mortality fell by
`r f1(key[["pct_decline"]])`% between the `r P1d` and `r PLd` cohorts. But the
relative gap between districts did not narrow. A cluster of districts in
`r sc_provinces` carried excess risk in the `r sc_cohorts` cohorts. A modest
district effect remained after adjustment for measured characteristics.

## Progress without convergence

The absence of convergence is the key finding. Absolute gaps narrowed only
because national mortality fell. The posterior dispersion between districts
stayed the same. No space-time interaction improved on a model with separate
spatial and time effects. The excess risk in Karnali and Sudurpashchim agrees
with earlier work. Relative inequalities in under-five mortality widened in
Nepal between 1996 and 2011 [@sreeramareddy2013]. Childhood mortality was
highest in Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces [@ghimire2019fa]. The same
region has persistent disadvantage in stunting [@nepali2022] and diarrhoea
[@li2020]. Similar persistence despite national decline has been reported in
sub-Saharan Africa [@golding2017; @burstein2019; @zondi2023; @fenta2025]. A
district that stays well above a halving national rate has not caught up.
National averages cannot show this.

## Methodological lessons

The choice of estimator mattered. Single-cohort district rates, based on about
100 births each, gave inconsistent evidence of clustering. Moran's I was
significant in `r nw(sum(mper_raw$moran_p < 0.05))` of four cohorts on crude
rates and in `r nw(sum(mper_eb$moran_p < 0.05))` on smoothed rates. Rates pooled
over the whole period were clearly clustered. Local cluster statistics on
sparse survey rates should therefore be read with caution, especially without
correction for multiple testing. Testing convergence within posterior samples
also mattered. Comparing posterior means would have suggested convergence
because of shrinkage alone.

## Predictors

The strongest predictors were multiple birth, a short preceding birth
interval, young maternal age, no maternal education and household poverty.
They agree with earlier NDHS analyses and systematic reviews [@ghimire2019;
@bhusal2022].
`r if (nrow(eth_hi) + nrow(eth_lo) > 0) "Differences by caste/ethnicity persisted after adjustment for wealth, education and residence [@ghimire2019fa]." else paste0("Unadjusted mortality was much higher among Dalit children (", f1(eth_u5("Dalit")), " per 1,000) than among Brahmin/Chhetri children (", f1(eth_u5("Brahmin/Chhetri")), "; Table 1). After adjustment for wealth, education and residence, no caste or ethnic group differed credibly. The caste gap therefore appears to run mainly through these factors [@ghimire2019fa].")`
These odds ratios come from one mutually adjusted model. They describe
associations and should not all be read as causal effects [@westreich2013].

Excluding children ever born and household size mattered. Both are strong
correlates of child death in many DHS studies. In some machine-learning
studies, household size ranks among the leading predictors [@naznin2025]. But
both are measured after the death and are changed by it. Including them would
largely reproduce the outcome rather than explain it.

## Machine learning

Flexible models gave little improvement over penalised logistic regression.
This agrees with systematic evidence from clinical prediction
[@christodoulou2019]. It is far below the near-perfect accuracy reported in
some DHS studies [@naznin2025]. Such figures can arise when related children
are split between training and test data. They can also arise when accuracy is
used as the metric for a rare outcome. In this study, all records of a child
stayed together, the test set was used once, and whole provinces were held
out. Segment-level AUROC is also inflated, because risk depends strongly on age.
For each child's risk of dying before age five, discrimination was low (AUROC
`r f2(min(perf_ch$roc_auc))`--`r f2(max(perf_ch$roc_auc))`). None of the models
could identify individual children at high risk.

The value of the models was explanatory. They transferred across provinces.
Each predictor contributed similarly to risk in every province. Predictors
therefore appear to act nationally. The persistent geographical gap is not
explained only by differences in household risk factors.

## Residual district variation

After adjustment for all measured child, maternal and household
characteristics, the median OR between districts was
`r f2(mor_d$median_odds_ratio)`. Between clusters within districts it was
`r f2(mor_c$median_odds_ratio)`. The district effect is modest compared with
the strongest individual associations. But it is credibly above zero, and it
applies to every child in a district. It may reflect area factors that the DHS
does not measure. Examples are travel time to emergency obstetric and newborn
care, staffing, referral capacity and seasonal isolation. These are hypotheses,
not findings. Linking survey data to health-facility and access data is a
priority for future work.

## Implications for policy

Districts in the detected cluster, and those with high exceedance
probabilities, form a priority list that accounts for uncertainty. Exceedance
probabilities are better than rankings of point estimates, because district
estimates differ greatly in precision. Predictors acted similarly across
provinces. This supports one common package of interventions, delivered more
intensively where risk is highest. The package should include birth spacing,
prevention of adolescent pregnancy, maternal education and care for multiple
births`r if (credible("^clean_fuelPolluting")) ", together with clean cooking fuel" else ""`.
The residual district effect suggests that investment in services and access is
also needed. The rising neonatal share means that further gains depend
increasingly on care around birth and in the first month.

At 33 per 1,000 in the 2022 NDHS, national under-five mortality is still above
Nepal's 2025 milestone of 24 and its 2030 target of 20 [@ndhs2022; @npc2017].
The relative gap between districts has not narrowed. Even if Nepal reaches its
national target, the highest-risk districts, with relative risks up to
`r f1(max(rr_last$rr))`, would remain well above it unless their decline
accelerates.

## Strengths and limitations

The study has several strengths. The discrete-time survival design uses
recently born children without treating them as survivors. One analytic file
was used for mortality estimation, spatial modelling and machine learning. The
estimates were checked against published NDHS values. Convergence was tested
with full posterior uncertainty. The validation designs respected the
clustering of the data.

The study also has limitations. First, mothers reported births up to ten years
back, so dates and ages at death may be misremembered. Children of women who
died or migrated are missing, which may bias mortality downward. Results were
similar, however, for births in the last five years. Second, the outer cohorts
rest on one survey each. The latest cohort is heavily censored: only
`r formatC(recent_obs, format = "f", digits = 0)`% of children born in
`r PLd` had died or reached age five by interview. Third, most covariates,
including wealth, were measured at interview rather than at birth. Fourth,
antenatal, delivery and postnatal care could not be included. Fifth, the
Bayesian and machine-learning models were not weighted. However, residence and
location, on which the survey strata are based, were included, and a
survey-weighted model gave similar results. Sixth, estimates are for districts,
while services are now run by 753 local governments. The two unsampled
districts are model estimates only. Seventh, the settings used in
leave-one-province-out validation were tuned on data from all provinces, which
may slightly favour those results. Finally, the study is observational and
cannot show causal effects.

# Conclusions

Under-five mortality in Nepal fell by `r f1(key[["pct_decline"]])`% between the
`r P1d` and `r PLd` birth cohorts. But the relative gap between districts did
not narrow. A cluster of districts in `r sc_provinces` carried excess risk in
the `r sc_cohorts` cohorts. The predictors of child death were the same across
provinces. A modest district effect remained after adjustment. Machine learning
did not improve prediction over penalised regression. Reaching Nepal's national
target of 20 per 1,000 by 2030 will need more intensive investment in
persistently high-risk districts. That investment should be guided by
estimates that show their uncertainty, and by research that links survey data
to health-service access.
